procedural_history.originating_court: Court of the Sub-Judge II Class, Mansa, in Case No. 134 of 1947.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Decree dated the 27th June, 1950, of the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: First Appeal No. 61 of 1948 from the District Judge, Bhatinda, arising out of the Judgment and Decree dated the 19th November, 1941, of the Court of the Subordinate Judge, I Class, Bhatinda, in Case No. 157 of 1942. The High Court dismissed the appeal on the ground that possession was under an arrangement between the co-sharers and no question of adverse possession could arise.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Appeal from the Judgment and Decree dated the 27th June, 1950, of the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad. The Supreme Court held that there was no force in the appeal and dismissed it with costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether the plea of adverse possession could arise when the possession was under an arrangement between the co-sharers.

facts: The possession of the property in question was held under an arrangement between the co-sharers.
law: A claim of adverse possession requires the possession to be hostile to the true owner's title.
Possession that is permissive, such as under an arrangement or agreement, is not considered hostile.
application: The High Court had previously decided the issue on the grounds that the possession was based on an arrangement between the co-sharers.
Because the possession was permissive and not hostile, the High Court concluded that a claim of adverse possession could not arise from these circumstances.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court affirmed the High Court's reasoning, holding that there was "no force" in the appeal. It concluded that a plea of adverse possession could not succeed because the possession was based on a permissive arrangement between the co-sharers, which negates the essential requirement of hostile possession.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the plea of adverse possession could arise when the possession was under an arrangement between the co-sharers.
appellant_arguments: The appellant, who was in possession of the property, implicitly argued that their possession had become adverse, thereby entitling them to ownership, despite the initial arrangement.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that the possession was under an arrangement between the co-sharers. Therefore, the possession was permissive and not hostile, and no question of adverse possession could arise under such circumstances.

cases.principle: The custom of pre-emption, when adopted by non-Muslims, can either follow the rules of Mahomedan Law or vary from it, being peculiar to the village's specific customs which originated from agreements among shareholders.

The law of pre-emption is a purely personal law, not an incident of property, and is enforceable only against persons who belong to a particular religious community or district where the custom is prevalent.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a right of pre-emption rests upon custom, it becomes the lex loci (the law of the place) and affects all lands situated in that place, irrespective of the religion, nationality, or domicile of the owners, unless specific incidents limiting its application are proven to be a part of the custom itself. The right of pre-emption is a real right that attaches to the land, not a personal right. A custom of pre-emption, once established, is presumed to be co-extensive with the Muhammadan Law on the subject unless the contrary is shown.
obiter: The right of pre-emption can be created by statute or by contract.
Where the law of pre-emption is not territorial or customary, it is applicable between Muhammadans as part of their personal law, administered on grounds of justice, equity, and good conscience.
In some provinces, the right of pre-emption is not recognized at all, even amongst Muhammadans, except on the footing of a custom.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court held that a plea of adverse possession cannot succeed when the possession in question originated from and was maintained under an arrangement between co-sharers. Such possession is considered permissive, not hostile, and therefore cannot meet the essential requirements for an adverse possession claim.
legal_tests_applied: For a claim of adverse possession to succeed, the possession must be hostile to the true owner's title. Possession that is permissive, such as that under an arrangement between co-sharers, is not considered hostile.
why_appellant_lost: The court found 'no force' in the appeal, thereby affirming the High Court's finding that the appellant's possession was not adverse because it was based on an arrangement between the co-sharers.
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully argued that the possession was permissive because it was 'under an arrangement between the co-sharers,' and the court agreed that 'no question of adverse possession could arise under the circumstances.'
